summary: Discovery call covering BlueHarbor's requirements for a private Redwood deployment across multi-region AWS + Azure, network onramp options (Transit Gateway, VPC peering, PrivateLink/Private Endpoint), egress/ingress constraints, cross-account peering, and compliance needs. Key concerns: regional data residency in EU and APAC, cross-cloud private connectivity, routing asymmetry, IP management, and certificates/KMS for HSM-managed keys. Agreed next steps: share network diagrams, Redwood to send checklist and pricing, schedule deep technical call on transit & firewall options.
topics: KMS/HSM and key management for models
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-18 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Evan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Jules Tran (Redwood CSM), Carlos Menendez (BlueHarbor Head of Platform), Priya Rao (BlueHarbor SRE), Alex Chen (BlueHarbor Security), Nadia Ortiz (BlueHarbor Cloud Architect)
---
00:00 Evan Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm evan with redwood inference, i'll kick us off. can folks introduce themselves quick?
00:08 Carlos Menendez: carlos, head of platform at blueharbor. we've been evaluating hosted but leaning private due to data residency and telemetry requirements.
00:14 Priya Rao: priya, SRE, mainly focused on network and ops. we've got hybrid cloud across aws and azure.
00:19 Alex Chen: alex, security — compliance, KMS, audit logs are our big asks.
00:24 Nadia Ortiz: nadia, cloud architect, will share diagrams later.
00:27 Maya Singh: maya from redwood, i'll cover technical design and transit options.
00:30 Evan Park: great. quick agenda: network onramp choices, region constraints, routing patterns, and security/keys. then next steps. sound good?
00:35 Carlos Menendez: yep
00:40 Evan Park: okay starting with your current infra — priya, can you describe where your workloads live and how you expect to call inference?
00:46 Priya Rao: sure — our primary data plane is in AWS us-east-1 and eu-west-1 for analytics pipelines, we also have a set of model preproc services in azure centralus for certain customers. low-latency inference is required from eu-west for EU customers, while APAC will be a later phase. right now we want a private onramp that avoids internet egress for model input data. ideally a VPC peering or private endpoint into redwood.
01:10 Maya Singh: got it. so two main dimensions: single-cloud private peering (vpc peering in aws) vs a transit hub (transit gateway or equivalent) for multi-account/multi-region, and cloud-provider private endpoints like aws privatelink or azure private endpoint which give service-managed endpoints. any preference?
01:29 Carlos Menendez: preference is minimal blast radius — we want to avoid wide-open routing and prefer cross-account peering through a central transit where we can inspect flows. but cost is a factor.
01:39 Priya Rao: also NAT egress costs are a concern, we have heavy tokenized telemetry so if every payload goes out to internet it's expensive.
01:46 Alex Chen: from security, we require that data entering redwood for EU customers never egress to non-EU regions. so routing and region pins are mandatory. we also want HSM-backed KMS for model keys.
01:57 Maya Singh: nodded — redwood private supports region pinning and we can deploy a dedicated control plane in your region. for keys we integrate with customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS with external key store or HSM via CloudHSM) and redwood can be configured to use it for model encryption at rest.
02:14 Evan Park: quick clarification — when you say "private endpoint" are you imagining a private service endpoint (like AWS Privatelink) or a full L3 peering?
02:21 Nadia Ortiz: we were thinking private service endpoint to reduce routing complexity, but we worry about limits like ENI quotas and cross-region availability. also some of our traffic originates from on-prem via VPN, so ip overlap is a risk.
02:36 Maya Singh: good point — Privatelink (AWS) creates ENIs in your VPC which can hit ENI limits; transit gateway avoids per-service ENIs but has its own cost model. For cross-region calls we can either set up regional redwood instances and route to the nearest region or use inter-region peering which has egress costs.
02:54 Carlos Menendez: curious about cross-cloud — can redwood stitch an azure private endpoint into an aws-hosted redwood pod?
03:02 Maya Singh: natively no single private endpoint spans clouds. typical approaches: 1) run redwood private in each cloud region you need and sync via the control plane, or 2) use a cloud network transit (e.g., SD-WAN or partner fabric) to bridge the provider private networks, but that's extra ops.
03:20 Alex Chen: does redwood support bringing your own IP (BYOIP) for the endpoints? we need predictable IPs for our firewall allowlists.
03:27 Maya Singh: we support static IPs for egress via NAT gateways in private deployments; BYOIP is more involved but we've done similar via customer's egress NAT prefixes on dedicated appliances. we'll need to scope that.
03:38 Priya Rao: what about routing asymmetry — if request goes to eu-west redwood instance but response routes back through on-prem, we have stateful firewalls that might drop it. can you guarantee symmetric routing?
03:50 Maya Singh: we can't control your on-prem routing, but recommended pattern is to use hub-and-spoke with transit gateway and central NAT/gateway so flows are symmetric. we'll share topology templates.
04:03 Evan Park: let's dig into region constraints — alex noted EU-only for EU customers. do you have a list of which datasets/customers need residency?
04:12 Alex Chen: yes — EU-regulated customers (finance, healthcare) must stay in EU; APAC customers will be Singapore and Tokyo later for latency. for now we need eu-west/ireland and azure-eu regions.
04:25 Carlos Menendez: and we have contractual SLAs so we need zones of control in each region for audit trails.
04:31 Maya Singh: redwood Private can be deployed into your VPCs per region. control plane can be private or run in our managed control plane in a waiting-to-be-agreed model; customers with strict residency usually want a private control plane too.
04:43 Nadia Ortiz: what's the lifting for private control plane? we have limited ops team.
04:48 Maya Singh: there's an ops package — private control plane is a customer-managed service we ship as IaC + images. we provide runbooks and a limited managed support add-on. tends to add 2-4 FTE equivalent for initial onboarding but less once steady state.
05:02 Priya Rao: latency targets — we need p95 inference under 250ms for eu customers. can you guarantee that from a regional deployment?
05:10 Maya Singh: regionally yes — if we provision dedicated capacity in the same region you should hit that. shared hosted endpoints may have added network RTT. we usually benchmark with a small pilot.
05:18 Carlos Menendez: pilot would be good. but before that, we need to validate network throughput — what are your recommended bandwidths and MTU settings? we have jumbo frames internally.
05:29 Maya Singh: model token streams are usually small, but if you're pushing batched requests or embedding bulk uploads you might want 2-5 Gbps per node depending on concurrency. MTU — we've seen issues with path MTU blackholes; we recommend standard 1500 or test end-to-end with icmp/pmTU to avoid fragmentation.
05:46 Priya Rao: noted. one more: Azure Private Endpoint has DNS implications — how do you handle split-horizon DNS and service discovery?
05:54 Maya Singh: we provide DNS records for private endpoints and recommend conditional forwarding to the redwood DNS zone; we also support customer-run DNS servers. we'll produce a DNS integration doc.
06:05 Carlos Menendez: about security certifications — what do you provide for SOC2 and ISO? we need audit logs, identity federation, and detailed access records.
06:13 Evan Park: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II and has ISO attestation for our hosted control plane; for private deployments we can enable audit logging into your SIEM and integrate with SAML/SSO and SCIM for user provisioning.
06:26 Alex Chen: for key management, can you use our KMS with external key store? we need HSM-backed keys and key usage audit.
06:33 Maya Singh: yes — we can integrate with AWS KMS + CloudHSM or use Azure Key Vault with HSM. we require cross-account IAM roles to use customer keys, we have patterns in the checklist.
06:45 Nadia Ortiz: what about egress NAT placement — if redwood needs to pull model updates or call back to a central service in a different region, will that traffic egress our VPC?
06:55 Maya Singh: model updates are served from the model registry which can be colocated in-region at deployment time; if you want zero cross-region egress we can pin image/model registry mirrors in each region. any remaining control-plane telemetry can be routed over private peering.
07:12 Priya Rao: do you support private peering with on-prem via our transit gateway? we use an AWS TGW+VPN to connect on-prem.
07:20 Maya Singh: yes — we can peer into your TGW, we typically create a spoke in your account and attach to TGW. we need routing tables and account IDs. for azure we use vNet peering or expressroute circuits.
07:33 Carlos Menendez: are there known pitfalls you see with cross-account peering and route propagation?
07:39 Maya Singh: common issues: overlapping CIDRs, missing route propagation on TGW, security group/NSG rules blocking ENIs, and reliance on DNS not forwarding correctly. also error cases when customers try to use internet-facing load balancers together with privatelink causing hairpin issues.
07:55 Alex Chen: does redwood create consumer ENIs (privatelink) in our account or do you manage those?
07:59 Maya Singh: for AWS Privatelink, the ENIs are created in your account, attached to subnets you designate. for private deployments we typically prefer that so you retain control. but again ENI quotas matter.
08:12 Priya Rao: what's the typical timeline to stand up a private region deployment?
08:16 Maya Singh: baseline deployment into a single region with a private control plane is 3-4 weeks for a standard config. multi-region multi-cloud is 6-10 weeks depending on approvals and network prep.
08:27 Carlos Menendez: cost drivers? we want a rough sense: dedicated nodes, transit gateway charges, privatelink fees, egress charges.
08:35 Evan Park: main drivers: instance hours for dedicated inference nodes, network transit (TGW per-hour + per-GB), privatelink per-hour and per-GB, storage for model registry, and support/ops. we'll send a model estimate in the pricing sheet.
08:47 Nadia Ortiz: any limits on concurrent model versions or can we pin heavy models per region?
08:52 Maya Singh: you can pin model versions and allocate dedicated pools per region; concurrent versions are limited by node capacity but there's no hard product cap. we can reserve capacity for important models.
08:59 Carlos Menendez: let's talk about failover — if eu region has an outage, what's the recommended failover path without violating data residency?
09:07 Maya Singh: for EU-only data, failover should be within other EU regions; we recommend multi-eu-region deployment (e.g., eu-west-1 + eu-central-1) with canary failover and automatic routing policy. cross-region failover to non-EU is possible but must be disabled for EU-regulated customers.
09:22 Alex Chen: how do you prove that data never left EU for audits? we need logs.
09:27 Maya Singh: audit logs capture request and model location metadata. for private deployments logs can be forwarded to your SIEM; we also provide retention controls. we'll include an audit evidence template.
09:40 Priya Rao: networking -- what about transitive peering limitations? we don't want to create peering mesh.
09:46 Maya Singh: avoid a full mesh; use hub-and-spoke (TGW or Azure Virtual WAN) for transitive routing. many customers use a dedicated networking account for connectivity.
09:56 Carlos Menendez: DNS split-horizon again — if we have internal users that should resolve redwood.internal and external users should hit public endpoints, any recommendations?
10:04 Maya Singh: conditional forwarding and private hosted zones work. for Azure you can use DNS private zones with links to vNets. bring your own resolver is also okay.
10:12 Evan Park: quick pause — any blockers or must-haves before we send pricing?
10:17 Alex Chen: KMS integration and proof of HSM usage is a must. also restricted egress for EU data and support contract SLAs.
10:25 Carlos Menendez: and a clear runbook for network changes. we have change windows and need low-risk steps.
10:30 Maya Singh: we'll add those to the checklist and SLA addendum.
10:34 Evan Park: ok, let's do a short demo of a sample topology — maya?
10:38 Maya Singh: (screen share described) here's a sample hub-and-spoke with TGW, redwood spokes in eu-west, and privatelink for our control plane. shows route tables and accepted routes.
11:02 Priya Rao: in the diagram, where are NATs for egress?
11:06 Maya Singh: NATs sit in a central services subnet in the hub; that gives single egress IPs for firewall allowlisting.
11:13 Carlos Menendez: looks good. question: for azure, what's the equivalent of TGW?
11:18 Maya Singh: Azure Virtual WAN or Azure Firewall Manager patterns, and expressroute for on-prem. we'll provide best-practice patterns in the doc.
11:27 Nadia Ortiz: any constraints for on-prem high-throughput calls? we have some customers with 10 Gbps links — will redwood nodes accept that without throttling?
11:36 Maya Singh: throughput per node depends on model size and concurrency; network stack supports high throughput but you need enough nodes and proper NIC sizing. we can run a performance test during pilot.
11:46 Carlos Menendez: about cross-account IAM — what permissions do we need to grant for KMS / STS?
11:52 Maya Singh: we need a role to decrypt keys for model loading (with customer key policy allowing redwood service principal) and an assume-role for the control plane to manage ENIs and autoscaling if you permit. we'll provide minimal permission templates.
12:07 Alex Chen: SCIM and SSO — we use Okta. can we provision redwood users into our IdP?
12:12 Evan Park: yes, we support SAML SSO + SCIM for user provisioning. for private control plane you can host the auth endpoint in your network and tie into Okta.
12:21 Priya Rao: any gotchas with MTU when using VPN+TGW+Azure?
12:25 Maya Singh: fragmentation and PMTU discovery fail often; recommend end-to-end testing and patching MSS / TCP MSS adjustments. we'll include an MTU checklist.
12:35 Carlos Menendez: costs again — do you have a rough ballpark for transit vs privatelink per TB?
12:41 Evan Park: depends on cloud: AWS privatelink charges per-GB + per-hour endpoint; TGW charges per-hour + per-GB. we'll send a comparison table with assumptions.
12:52 Nadia Ortiz: what about support during onboarding — do you run the initial connectivity steps?
12:57 Jules Tran: CSM here — we run a joint onboarding plan. we do a connectivity workshop, provide runbooks, and can do some hands-on support for the first two weeks.
13:08 Priya Rao: great. final question: blackbox managed updates — will redwood ever pull models from a public repo? we need guaranteed model artifact locality.
13:16 Maya Singh: we won't pull from public internet unless you opt-in. default is a mirrored model registry inside your network or in-region artifacts.
13:25 Carlos Menendez: sounds good. let's recap next steps.
13:29 Evan Park: recap — we'll send checklist + pricing, maya will schedule a deep technical session on transit/fwrules, blueharbor will share network diagrams and CIDRs, alex will send KMS/HSM requirements. anything else?
13:41 Alex Chen: include audit log schema and retention options.
13:45 Evan Park: done. thanks all. we'll follow up by EOW.
13:50 Carlos Menendez: thanks everyone, bye.
